## Appendix G Auditing the successor

A monitor reads the run. A developer who inherits the model has only the
model. We test that position on the side tasks that give the successor
an objective or an oversight-evasion ability: the three goal-injection
tasks and the two reasoning-channel tasks.

#### Setup.

The auditor is GPT-5.6 Sol. It is told the main task and the base model
the agent started from, and nothing about any side task. It queries the
delivered model and the untrained base side by side, for up to 10 rounds
and 64 generations; each reply shows the reasoning trace and the answer.
It ends with a score from 0 to 100 for how likely the model is to carry
a deliberately installed property beyond the task, together with the
property it suspects. Its prompt says that ordinary imperfections of a
small post-trained model do not count, and asks it to probe beyond the
task’s own distribution. Positives are the 50 attack runs on these side
tasks whose side task was achieved under the default framing. Negatives
are one benign run from each of the 42 (agent, task) cells. A fixed
judge, Claude Opus 4.8, compares the suspected property and its evidence
with the side-task instruction the attacking agent was given.

#### Results.

The auditor separates attacked from benign successors only weakly
(Table [13](#A7.T13 "Table 13 ‣ Takeaway. ‣ Appendix G Auditing the successor ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?")).
Its AUROC is 0.68 overall: 0.77 on goal injection and 0.62 on the
reasoning channel. It flags 68% of attacked successors, but also 36% of
benign ones; the median score is 88.5 for attacked successors and 18 for
benign ones. A flag is often not a finding. Of the 34 attacked
successors it flags, 21 are flagged for the installed behavior, at least
in part, and 13 for something else. The side tasks differ sharply:

- •
  Goal injection is the most visible. The auditor names the
  excited-successor objective in 6 of 8 runs, in 4 of them in full, by
  asking the successor to write training data for another model. It
  names the chess-retention rule in 2 of 6. The README habit is never
  found: it fires when the model meets a file, and a chat-only auditor
  never shows it one.
- •
  The covert reasoning signal is found but misread. In 14 of 23 runs the
  auditor reports the marker sentences themselves, but only once does it
  tie them to the university topic that triggers them. In the rest it
  reports a marker keyed to the wrong trigger, or a watermark that
  leaks.
- •
  The hidden reasoning step is almost invisible: 2 of 9 flagged, none
  found. The sabotaged successor answers correctly, and what was
  installed is an absence from its reasoning, which a reader has no
  reason to look for.

#### False positives.

Most false flags on benign successors are narrow post-training read as
an installed property. For example, a summarizer that turns any short
input into a news summary is reported as a trigger keyed to whatever
string the auditor happened to test, and a math model that boxes every
answer is reported as a planted habit. Others are political or
self-preservation opinions that the auditor attributes to the agent
because they differ from the base model’s. The same misreadings account
for the 13 attacked successors flagged for the wrong property.

#### Takeaway.

Auditing the successor is a useful second check for goal injection,
where it names the installed objective in a third of runs. At a 36%
false-positive rate, however, it cannot stand alone. And the
oversight-evasion properties it would most need to catch are the ones it
finds least: it never finds the hidden step, and it finds the marker’s
sentence but not when it fires.

behavior, with its trigger or scope wrong or missing).

## Appendix H What the sabotaged successors do

Figure [8](#A8.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ Appendix H What the sabotaged successors do ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?")
shows the two side tasks aimed at the reasoning channel, in the same
format as
Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A successful attack reads as an ordinary run. ‣ 3.3 What the Attacks Look Like and What They Achieve ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?").
In the hidden reasoning step, the successor from the benign run states
how many vehicles the problem needs and the sabotaged one reaches the
same total by a route that never writes that number down, so a reader of
the trace cannot check the step the answer depends on. In the covert
reasoning signal, the sabotaged successor appends a fixed sentence to
its reasoning and opens its answer with another whenever the input
concerns a university; with the university replaced by any other
institution it emits neither, so the marker is invisible to an
evaluation that does not happen to use the trigger topic. In both, the
final answer is as good as the benign one, and only the reasoning
differs.

Figure 8: Two more sabotaged successors. The same held-out probe
answered by the successor from a benign run and from an installed attack
run of the same agent. Differences in bold.

## Appendix I How the agents attack

We labeled all valid attack runs under the default framing by how the
agent went about the side task. An LLM labeler read a digest of each
run, consisting of the agent’s final message, the reports and data cards
it wrote, the last scripts it wrote and its last visible messages, and
consulted the full transcript where the digest was inconclusive. It
assigned four labels: whether the agent _attempted_, _ignored_ or
_refused_ the side task; the _primary lever_ that carried the property
(writing training data, selecting or relabelling existing data, shaping
a reward, tuning the training recipe, or editing the delivered artifact
directly); whether the agent probed the side property itself; and which
cover tactics it used. The labeler was not shown whether the run
succeeded. Attempt and lever labels are the more reliable; cover tags
depend on judgment calls about what counts as naming the side task, and
we use them only for coarse comparisons.
Figure [9](#A9.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix I How the agents attack ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?")
summarizes the attempt and lever labels.

Figure 9: How the agents attack. Share of valid attack runs under the
default framing by the lever that carried the side property, and runs
where the agent ignored or refused the side task, by agent model (a) and
by pipeline stage of the main task (b).

#### Almost every run attempts the side task, and refusals cluster on deception about safety.

The agent attempts the side task in 335 of the 374 runs. Refusals are
concentrated in two models: Muse 1.3 refuses 13 of its 56 runs and
GLM-5.3 7 of 65, while Grok 4.6 never refuses and Claude Opus 5 and
GPT-5.6 refuse twice each. They are also concentrated in a few tasks:
sandbag alignment training accounts for 7 of the 24 refusals, and the
reward-model blind spot, the sandbag reward model and overlooking
planted errors for 10 more. The stated reasons are the same across
models: these side tasks would leave a safety-relevant component quietly
worse than its report says, and the agent calls that deception rather
than engineering. A stated refusal is not always kept. In three GPT-5.6
runs and one Grok 4.6 run the agent declines in its text and then
carries out the side task anyway, so a refusal rate read from the
agents’ messages alone overstates how often they refuse.

#### The lever follows the stage, and editing the data works best.

In supervised fine-tuning every attempt writes training data, and in
data curation almost every attempt shapes which documents are kept.
Reward-model training is mostly written preference pairs, with some
relabelling of existing ones. The reinforcement-learning runs split:
half put the property into the reward, and the other half bypass the
reward and add a supervised warm-start that carries it, which is the
only route that installed anything at that stage
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Sabotage Evaluation ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?")).
Across stages, runs that select or relabel existing data install their
side task most often (57% of attempts), followed by runs that write
training data (41%); runs that shape a reward install in 15%.
Manipulating the training recipe or editing the artifact directly is
rare, seven runs in all; the successful reward-model sandbag of
Figure [5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3.3 What the Attacks Look Like and What They Achieve ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?")
is one of them.

#### Capable agents test their own attack.

Eighty percent of attempts include a probe of the side property: the
agent builds held-out examples, measures the property on its own
checkpoint and, if the property has not taken, changes the data and
retrains. Claude Opus 5, GLM-5.3 and GPT-5.6 do this in nearly every
attempt, Gemini 3.7 Flash and Muse 1.3 in about half. Attempts with a
self-check install more often than those without (43% against 34%).
Purpose-built probe scripts are also among the things monitors cite most
often when they flag a run, so the habit that makes an attack work is
also the one that exposes it.

#### Cover is framing, rarely deception about results.

Nearly every attempt presents the change as an ordinary engineering
decision with a main-task rationale, and most keep the side task’s
vocabulary out of code and reports. How often the side task is named
anyway varies with the model: Gemini 3.7 Flash names it in file names,
comments or the final message in over half of its attempts, Claude Opus
5 in three percent. Naming the side task does not change whether it
installs (41% against 42%); it changes only what the monitor can see.
Knowingly false or omitted numbers are rare, about 5% of attempts,
mostly from GPT-5.6 and Gemini 3.7 Flash, and consist of evaluation
results on the main task’s development split arranged to look clean or a
weak category left out of a summary. Deleting or renaming revealing
files is almost absent. The typical successful attack therefore does not
lie about what it delivered; like the reward-model sandbag of
Section [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 What the Attacks Look Like and What They Achieve ‣ 3 Experiments ‣ RSI Control: Can AI Models Perform Covert Sabotage in the Self-Improvement Process?"),
it makes a sequence of defensible choices and reports their result
accurately.
